description: Six final-year Computer Engineering students from ITBA in Buenos Aires. We like building fast and making things that look good and actually work.
summary:
Dumpsite is a platform that finds open-air dumps that are still in use, with radar images from NASA's NISAR satellite.

NISAR images the same place every 12 days, day or night and through clouds. A dump in use keeps changing because waste keeps arriving, so we measure how often each spot changes more than the land around it. A LightGBM model, trained on radar spots labeled with a catalog of 66,981 known dumps, then classifies each changing spot as a dump or something else. We ran it on Argentina and 29 other regions and found 183 possible new dumps that are not in any public catalog.

New dumps appear faster than anyone can map them, and in Argentina there is no official list of where they are or which ones are still active. Dumpsite shows this on a public map, so agencies and municipalities can decide where to send inspectors.
details:
Dumpsite looks for open-air dumps that are still in use. It works with radar images from NASA's NISAR satellite, which passes over the same place every 12 days, day or night and through clouds. Radar coherence tells how much a place looks alike between two passes. A dump in use changes all the time because trucks keep bringing waste and machines keep moving soil, so its coherence drops much more than in the land around it. Each time the radar passes, we check if a spot changed more than its surroundings. The Insomnia index is how often that happened. Water and farmland also change for their own reasons, so we leave them out first.

The radar can tell that a place changes. It can't tell what the place is, and a quarry or an airfield can change just as much as a dump. So we joined OpenStreetMap, Climate TRACE, the US EPA landfill list and the methane plumes seen by NASA's EMIT into one catalog of 66,981 known dumps, and we added places that also change often, like quarries and airfields. A LightGBM model, trained on radar spots labeled with that catalog, looks at 29 variables from the radar and from Sentinel-2 images, such as vegetation, bare soil, water and shape, and classifies each changing spot as a dump or something else.

We ran it on Argentina and 29 other regions in the US, Mexico, India and Indonesia. The model found 183 possible new dumps that are not in any public catalog. They appear in yellow on a public map at dumpsite.earth, next to the known dumps. Clicking a site opens its satellite image and what the radar saw on every pass. There is also a list of all the sites that anyone can download to compare what the records say with what the radar sees.

In Argentina there is no official list of where the open dumps are or which ones are still active, and checking them on the ground takes time and money. NISAR data is free and covers the whole planet. Dumpsite can help environmental agencies and municipalities decide where to send inspectors first, and it can show when a dump that was closed on paper is still being used. The same method works anywhere NISAR passes, so the next step is to run it on the rest of the world.

Most dump mapping uses optical images of a single day. We look at how a place behaves over months of radar passes, because a dump in use never looks the same twice. That idea let us find dumps that nobody had mapped before.

We wrote the processing in Python with NumPy, pandas, rasterio, shapely and LightGBM. NISAR data comes from NASA's ASF DAAC, Sentinel-2 from Microsoft Planetary Computer and the water mask from the JRC Global Surface Water dataset. The web is built with React, TypeScript, Vite and MapLibre over NASA GIBS imagery. We made the videos with Remotion. We used AI tools to write code faster. The opening clip of the video is AI-generated and marked on screen, and the English narration is a synthetic voice (Azure AI Speech).

We only used open data and the code is public. Every number in the video and on the map comes from a file in the repository. We call these sites possible dumps because nobody has visited them yet, and a change in the radar alone is not proof. The heavy processing is done ahead of time, so the map loads quickly.

Everyone shown in the video is an adult team member who agreed to appear.
